content: The guidelines for stopping mass drug administration (MDA) and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis were developed through a rigorous process. The draft guidelines were subjected to external peer review before finalization, during which no changes to the recommendations were allowed, but clarifications were added. The Guideline Development Group (GDG), consisting of seven members and three methodologists, all signed WHO Declaration of Interest forms. Two members disclosed receiving research grants or consulting fees from the Mectizan Donation Program or the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. These interests were reviewed by the WHO Steering Group, which determined they did not constitute significant conflicts of interest, allowing full participation in the guideline development process. The guidelines emphasize the use of O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) testing in black flies to demonstrate the interruption of transmission of Onchocerca volvulus in populations receiving MDA. This test was rated highly accurate with strong evidence, particularly in distinguishing O. volvulus from other parasites. The rationale for its recommendation is its high specificity and cost-effectiveness when using larger pools of flies. However, its implementation depends on factors such as procurement policies, support from health ministries, and community engagement. The Ov-16 serology test is recommended for use in children under 10 years of age to demonstrate the interruption of transmission. This test is minimally invasive, cost-effective, and suitable for field use with strong community participation. However, its evidence quality is rated low due to limitations in studies conducted in high-prevalence settings and the imperfect reference standard (skin snip microscopy). The test should be used alongside O-150 PCR testing, particularly when PCR results are near the threshold for transmission interruption. Skin snip microscopy, while historically used, is no longer recommended for demonstrating transmission interruption due to its low sensitivity in low-prevalence settings and redundancy in the presence of O-150 PCR testing. Ocular infection assessment, involving the detection of microfilariae in the anterior chamber of the eye, is not recommended due to its high cost, the need for specialized personnel, and limited evidence supporting its use in low-endemicity settings. Despite its diagnostic specificity, the undesirable consequences outweigh the benefits. Post-treatment surveillance (PTS) typically lasts 3–5 years and involves diagnostic tests such as O-150 PCR in black flies and, if necessary, Ov-16 serology in children. The surveillance period may be extended in areas co-endemic with lymphatic filariasis or where there is a risk of reinfection due to migration or cross-border issues. At the end of PTS, an independent national oversight committee reviews the data to confirm transmission interruption. If satisfied, the Ministry of Health prepares a country report for submission to WHO to initiate the verification process. The international verification team, constituted by WHO, independently assesses the country’s report to confirm the elimination of onchocerciasis.
